newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surprised but relieved at Peru hostage raid.
newsitem.headline: Japan surprised but relieved at Peru hostage raid.

text.p: Japan, initially surprised by a daring daytime commando raid to end a siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, breathed a deep sigh relief on Wednesday after all the Japanese hostages survived the ordeal.

"It's finally over," said Morimichi Aoki, son of Japanese ambassador to Peru, Morihisa Aoki. The ambassador was unharmed in the raid, along with all but one of the 71 other hostages held for more than four months by Marxist rebels.
"I was surprised force was used, but I was confident all along that it would come to a happy ending," his son said. "More than being worried, I was proud of my father."
Ambassador Aoki, 58, speaking at a news conference in Lima, said: "The first thing when I heard the explosion, like the time I heard them on the night of the party, I thought my life was at an end."

All Japanese television stations aired the raid live from Lima early on Wednesday and newspapers put out extra editions. Some relatives of hostages broke down in tears when they heard the release of their loved ones.
"I want to see my son as soon as possible," said Kazue Sugimaru, the mother of Masanori Sugimaru, 50, a travel agent held hostage along with ambassador Aoki.
"I was half expecting this, but was worried that the desperate guerillas might shoot randomly at the hostages," said Motohiro Saito, father of hostage Keiichi Saito.
"I can finally smile. Maybe I'll celebrate with wine tonight."
Japanese companies whose executives were among those held for the past four months expressed relief.
"We are very relieved that this long hostage situation has finally ended," said Toyota Motor Corp president Hiroshi Okuda.
"I express heartfelt sympathy for the hostage and soldiers who were killed," said Toshihiko Kawashima, public relations officer at Marubeni Corp.
"But I am glad that most of the hostages were safe and hope this will never happen again."
Tokyo residents appeared to support Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's decision to use force to end the crisis.
"I think the hostages were reaching their physical as well as mental limit. This was unavoidable measure," said Makoto Takehara, a 19-year-old student.
"I think President Fujimori is great," said Taeko Tsuneki, a 64-year-old housewife.
"Japanese politicians try to resolve problems with money, but that would only invite more terrorism. I feel sorry for the victims, but in this case, I support his choice of using military force."
